title: Clinician conscientious objection and referral
short_description: A patient requests a lawful abortion from a clinician who has a longstanding conscientious objection to providing abortions and also believes that making a direct referral would make the clinician complicit.
decision_question: When a clinician conscientiously refuses to provide a lawful abortion, what information, referral or facilitation duties should the health system require?
position_families: Permit refusal to provide but require advance notice, accurate unbiased information and timely direct referral or transfer
Permit refusal to provide and to make a morally implicating referral, while requiring the institution—not the individual objector—to supply an immediate alternative access pathway
Require provision in emergencies or when refusal/referral delay would otherwise make timely care unavailable
Stronger professional-role accounts under which accepting the role entails provision of standard care despite personal objection
Stronger conscience accounts under which neither provision nor facilitation may be compelled, subject to nondeception and emergency/non-abandonment limits

scenario: A patient requests a lawful abortion from a clinician who has a longstanding conscientious objection to providing abortions and also believes that making a direct referral would make the clinician complicit. Another qualified provider is available. For this benchmark, assume a direct referral or warm transfer can secure care within about two days, while requiring the patient to locate a provider without facilitation is likely to add roughly a week and may narrow available procedural options, although it is not expected to create an immediate medical emergency. The health system must decide what advance disclosure, unbiased information, referral or other access duties to require of the objecting clinician.
